title: Illness Crisis Hits UAE Team as Pogačar Chases Historic Fifth Tour de France Title
excerpt: Brandon McNulty abandoned the race on Stage 18, Adam Yates is battling gastrointestinal illness, and Tim Wellens barely survived the time cut — leaving Pogačar increasingly isolated ahead of the decisive Alpine stages.
body:
• Brandon McNulty abandoned the Tour de France during Stage 18 on Thursday, the latest blow to UAE Team Emirates-XRG, which is battling a wave of gastrointestinal illness.
  • Adam Yates has been struggling with stomach issues since Stage 16, while Tim Wellens finished last on Stage 18, surviving the time cut by just two minutes.
  • Race leader Tadej Pogačar maintains a 4:32 lead over Remco Evenepoel but faces the decisive Alpe d'Huez stages on Friday and Saturday with a depleted team.

McNulty's Exit Caps Nightmare Day for UAE

UAE Team Emirates-XRG's Tour de France campaign took a devastating turn on Thursday as American rider Brandon McNulty abandoned the race during Stage 18 from Voiron to Orcières-Merlette, according to CyclingUpToDate. McNulty, 28, is the latest casualty in what appears to be a gastrointestinal illness sweeping through the squad at the worst possible moment — with three gruelling Alpine stages still to come.

McNulty's departure came just days after he was knocked off his bike by an angry motorist in a road rage incident before the Stage 16 time trial in Evian-les-Bains on July 21. Team principal Mauro Gianetti told The Athletic at the time that the American's injuries were "nothing so big," and McNulty started the time trial on schedule. But the combination of that incident and illness proved too much.

"McNulty was such a valuable rider."

— Tadej Pogačar, in post-stage comments on NBC Sports

Yates Struggling, Wellens on the Edge

McNulty's exit is only part of the story. British rider Adam Yates, 33, a key mountain domestique for Pogačar who finished third at the Tour in 2023, has been battling an upset stomach since the Stage 16 time trial. He was seen dropping off the back of the main peloton about 100km into Wednesday's Stage 17 and eventually finished 26 minutes behind stage winner Jasper Philipsen, according to AFP.

On Stage 18, Yates managed to finish but visibly struggled throughout. Meanwhile, veteran Belgian Tim Wellens — a critical support rider who had been sent back on Stage 17 to help guide Yates to the finish — was himself the last rider across the line on Thursday, surviving the time limit by just two minutes, according to CyclingUpToDate.

"Yesterday he was really, really bad. If yesterday was a normal stage he wouldn't finish I think but luckily it was just a TT and he managed it. I have to say he looked terrible."

— Tadej Pogačar, on Adam Yates's condition, via AFP

Sports director Simone Pedrazzini acknowledged the severity of the situation. "Maybe he won't start tomorrow but maybe he can do two stages and then on Saturday be important for Tadej," Pedrazzini told AFP about Yates.

A Team Unravelling at the Critical Moment

The illness has struck UAE at the most punishing point of the race. CyclingUpToDate reported that "most likely, all riders are suffering from gastrointestinal issues, putting also at risk the health of Tadej Pogačar and Isaac del Toro." NBC Sports analysts have openly asked whether the team is "falling apart" heading into the final stages.

The losses compound earlier setbacks. On Stage 15, Del Toro and McNulty were both involved in a crash that broke two-time champion Jonas Vingegaard's collarbone and forced him out of the race. Del Toro was visibly struggling in the aftermath but has continued and sits third overall, 6 minutes and 51 seconds behind Pogačar.

Pogačar still holds a commanding 4:32 lead over Remco Evenepoel after Stage 18 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz take a solo victory, finishing 45 seconds ahead of Mauro Schmid. Pogačar rolled across the line in a group containing Evenepoel and Del Toro, with no changes to the general classification standings, according to Reuters.

Alpe d'Huez Looms With a Depleted Squad

The concern for Pogačar is what lies ahead. Friday's Stage 19 covers 127.9km from Gap to Alpe d'Huez, one of cycling's most iconic climbs. Saturday's Stage 20, described by Tour director Christian Prudhomme as "possibly the toughest mountain stage in Tour history," features 5,450 metres of climbing including the Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Télégraphe, Col du Galibier, and an unprecedented approach to Alpe d'Huez via the Col de Sarenne, according to Reuters.

In a fully healthy team, Pogačar would have multiple domestiques to control the pace on these climbs, chase down attacks, and deliver him to the final kilometres in prime position. Now, with McNulty gone, Yates a question mark, and Wellens barely surviving each stage, the Slovenian may have to rely heavily on Del Toro alone — or fend for himself entirely.

"I think nobody would really commit," Pogačar said of the relatively calm Stage 18, according to NBC Sports. But that dynamic is unlikely to hold on Alpe d'Huez, where Evenepoel — who won the Stage 16 time trial and has been the Tour's strongest rider behind Pogačar — will sense opportunity.

What to Watch

The final three stages will determine whether Pogačar can claim a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title despite his team's crisis. Stage 19 to Alpe d'Huez on Friday will be the first real test of his ability to survive without his usual mountain support. If Yates cannot start, and Wellens continues to fade, Pogačar's 4:32 lead will need to be defended on pure individual strength against a fully supported Evenepoel. The race concludes with Sunday's processional stage to the Champs-Élysées in Paris.
nri_angle: Global sporting drama relevant to cycling fans worldwide, with Pogačar's quest for a historic fifth title adding to the stakes.
